A.explanation: At P the voltmeter still includes the separate $3\text{ V}$ cell, so the reading is not $0\text{ V}$.

B.explanation: The reading at P is not zero because the $+$ lead at P and the $-$ lead are at different potentials due to the right-hand $3\text{ V}$ cell.

C.explanation: Moving the slider from P to Q adds the $3\text{ V}$ across the potentiometer, so the reading cannot stay at $3\text{ V}$.

D.explanation: At P the voltmeter reads the $3\text{ V}$ cell alone, and at Q it reads $3\text{ V} + 3\text{ V} = 6\text{ V}$ with the shown polarity.

hints: Notice the bottom wire is common: end P, the left cell lower terminal and the lower terminal of the right-hand $3\text{ V}$ cell are the same node.
Connect the potentiometer action to potential: $V_Q - V_P = 3\text{ V}$ from the left cell, so the slider potential rises by $3\text{ V}$ from P to Q.
Connect the voltmeter polarity to the right-hand cell: $V_{+} - V_{-}$ equals slider potential minus the upper terminal, which is $3\text{ V}$ below P.
walkthrough: Take $V_P = 0\text{ V}$ as reference because P is the common junction. The left $3\text{ V}$ cell is across the potentiometer with Q at the top, so $V_Q - V_P = 3\text{ V}$ and $V_Q = 3\text{ V}$.

The voltmeter $+$ lead is at the slider potential $V_S$. The $-$ lead connects through the right-hand $3\text{ V}$ cell to P, with the cell orientated so the $-$ lead is $3\text{ V}$ below P, so $V_{-} = V_P - 3\text{ V} = -3\text{ V}$.
Voltmeter reading is $V = V_{+} - V_{-} = V_S - (-3\text{ V}) = V_S + 3\text{ V}$.
At end P, $V_S = V_P = 0\text{ V}$, so $V = 0 + 3 = 3\text{ V}$.
At end Q, $V_S = V_Q = 3\text{ V}$, so $V = 3 + 3 = 6\text{ V}$.
The pair $3\text{ V}$ at P and $6\text{ V}$ at Q is option D.
